name: Flidais

sources: Clark, Rosalind. The Great Queens: Irish Goddesses from the Morrígan to Cathleen Ní Houlihan. Irish Literary Studies 34. Gerrards Cross: Colin Smythe, 1991, 31.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Flidais, written Flidas and Fliodhas as well, was an Irish goddess. Many lands of Europe had a woodland goddess much like her. She calls to mind the Greek Artemis, Diana of Rome, and Artio of the continental Celts. Flidais stood for fertility and abundance. She led the wild beasts, and her name means doe. She rode a chariot pulled by deer. She governed the home herds and owned a magical cow. That cow gave milk enough for thirty people each night. Her animal temper reached into her love life. She matched her consort Fergus Mac Roich in desire. When Flidais refused him, Fergus took seven ordinary women. Some tales join Flidais in marriage to the fairy Adammair. Nothing else is known of that husband. Her daughters shared her bold ways. Be Chuille was cast out of Fairyland for her free conduct. Be Teite was another wanton woman, though little legend of her remains. Fand, a wild fairy, stole the hero Cuchulainn away from his wife Emer.

okr.objective: Flidais is the Irish goddess of fertility whose name means doe.
key_results: Flidais resembled the Greek Artemis, the Roman Diana, and Artio.
